nodes.referent: The law of conservation of mass in chemistry: in an ordinary (non-nuclear) chemical reaction, the total mass of reactants equals the total mass of products -- matter is neither created nor destroyed. Not the relativistic mass-energy equivalence of physics, and not a general philosophical claim about the permanence of matter.
nodes.source_hint: General chemistry textbooks' treatment of the law of conservation of mass / stoichiometry; Encyclopedia Britannica entry on Antoine Lavoisier.
nodes.rationale: C1 edge-demand: conservation of mass is the foundational quantitative law of chemistry that anchors field:chemistry (already reviewed) and completes a theory-concept-plus-founder triangle with person:antoine-lavoisier, mirroring the natural-selection/Darwin and law-of-universal-gravitation/Newton pattern already in the corpus. C3: targets the specific physical law, not the discipline of chemistry.
nodes.uncertainty: Lavoisier is the standard chemistry-textbook credit for rigorously establishing the law via closed-vessel weighing experiments (1770s-1780s, Traite elementaire de chimie, 1789), but Mikhail Lomonosov is credited in some sources (particularly Russian historiography) with an earlier 1748-1756 formulation and closed-vessel experiment; this priority question is reflected in the founder edge's confidence and ambiguous flag, not the node's identity, which is unambiguous.

nodes.referent: The biological doctrine that (1) all living organisms are composed of one or more cells, (2) the cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life, and (3) cells arise only from pre-existing cells -- the unifying 19th-century theory of cell biology. Not any single model of a cell's internal structure, and not a specific technique such as cell culture.
nodes.source_hint: General biology textbooks' treatment of cell theory; Encyclopedia Britannica 'cell theory'.
nodes.rationale: C1 edge-demand: cell theory is the unifying 19th-century doctrine of subfield:cell-biology (already reviewed), and completes theory-concept-plus-co-founder triangles with person:theodor-schwann and person:matthias-jakob-schleiden, the two classically credited co-formulators. C3: a bounded scientific doctrine, matching the concept (not subfield) side of the movement/doctrine rule.
nodes.uncertainty: Cell theory is sometimes stated as a three-part doctrine, with the third part ('omnis cellula e cellula' -- all cells arise from pre-existing cells) usually credited to Rudolf Virchow (1855), who is not in this batch's endpoint list and so is not represented; this node therefore currently reflects only the Schwann/Schleiden (1838-1839) unification of plant and animal tissue as cellular, not the full later doctrine.

nodes.referent: The medical/microbiological theory that many diseases are caused by microorganisms (pathogens) invading a host -- established experimentally in the mid-to-late 19th century. Distinct from germ-plasm theory (August Weismann's theory of heredity via germ cells) and from germ-layer theory in embryology; 'germ' here means pathogenic microorganism, not reproductive cell.
nodes.source_hint: Encyclopedia Britannica 'germ theory'; general history-of-medicine references on the establishment of germ theory.
nodes.rationale: C1 edge-demand: germ theory of disease is the founding doctrine of subfield:microbiology (already reviewed), and completes theory-concept-plus-co-founder triangles with person:louis-pasteur and person:robert-koch, its two classically credited experimental founders. C3: a bounded scientific theory, matching the concept side of the movement/doctrine rule.
nodes.uncertainty: The label risks conflation with two unrelated 'germ' senses in biology -- germ-plasm theory and germ-layer theory -- addressed explicitly in the referent. Earlier speculative precursors (Fracastoro's 16th-century contagion hypothesis, Henle's 1840 arguments) existed but did not rise to experimental formalization, so they are not treated as competing founder claims here.

nodes.referent: The geological methodological principle that the same natural processes and laws observed operating today (erosion, sedimentation, volcanism, etc.) operated in the past at broadly similar rates, and can be used to explain the Earth's geological history ('the present is the key to the past') -- opposed historically to catastrophism. Not the general philosophical doctrine of uniformity of nature, and not a legal/political usage of the word.
nodes.rationale: C1 edge-demand: uniformitarianism is geology's founding methodological doctrine, anchoring subfield:geology (already reviewed) and completing theory-concept-plus-co-founder triangles with person:james-hutton (originator, 1785/1795) and person:charles-lyell (systematizer/popularizer, Principles of Geology, 1830). C3: a textbook example of a bounded doctrine under the movement/doctrine rule (contrasted historically with catastrophism), not a standing subfield of its own.
nodes.uncertainty: Hutton and Lyell are sequential, non-competing contributors (originator then systematic formalizer), not rival claimants, so there is no priority dispute to flag; the main residual risk is purely referent-identity (a resolver conflating the geological doctrine with the general philosophical 'uniformity of nature' principle), addressed in the referent.

nodes.referent: Entropy in thermodynamics: the state function measuring the unavailability of a system's energy to do work, central to the second law of thermodynamics (the entropy of an isolated system tends to increase) -- the classical/macroscopic thermodynamic quantity, as distinct from its later statistical-mechanical (microstate-counting) reformulation and from Shannon's unrelated information-theoretic 'entropy' of a probability distribution.
nodes.source_hint: General physics/thermodynamics textbooks' treatment of entropy and the second law; Encyclopedia Britannica 'entropy'.
nodes.rationale: C1 edge-demand: entropy is thermodynamics' central state function (the second law), anchoring subfield:thermodynamics (already reviewed) with a clean part_of edge; no founder edge is proposed because the candidate slate did not supply a person endpoint and no reviewed person node exists in this corpus for the physicist standardly credited with introducing the term. C3: a bounded physical concept, not a subfield of its own.
nodes.uncertainty: 'Entropy' names several related but formally distinct quantities across disciplines -- classical thermodynamic entropy, statistical-mechanical entropy, and Shannon's information-theoretic entropy -- and a resolver could plausibly match the wrong one; the referent restricts this node to the classical thermodynamic sense to match the candidate's stated field attachment.

nodes.referent: Herbert Simon's concept that real decision-makers have limited information, cognitive capacity, and time, and so 'satisfice' (seek a satisfactory, not optimal, outcome) rather than fully optimize as assumed by neoclassical rational-choice models -- a foundational critique/revision of the rational-actor assumption in economics and decision theory. Not general 'irrationality' and not a specific named cognitive bias.
nodes.source_hint: Nobel Prize committee citation for Herbert Simon (1978); general behavioral-economics textbooks' treatment of bounded rationality as a founding concept.
nodes.rationale: C1 edge-demand: bounded rationality is Herbert Simon's signature concept and completes a theory-concept-plus-founder triangle; the candidate itself names two possible disciplinary homes (economics or behavioral economics), and this batch resolves the part_of target to subfield:behavioral-economics as the more referent-precise choice (the concept is standardly presented as one of that subfield's founding ideas), flagged as a judgment call on the edge. C3: a bounded theoretical concept/critique, not a subfield of its own.
nodes.uncertainty: person:herbert-simon's domain in this corpus is cognitive_sciences, not social_sciences, reflecting his genuinely cross-disciplinary career (economics Nobel 1978, but also AI/cognitive-science work) -- this is a pre-existing corpus fact, not introduced by this proposal, and does not by itself argue for one part_of target over the other.

nodes.referent: Max Weber's methodological concept (Idealtypus) in sociology: an analytical construct built by one-sidedly accentuating certain features of a social phenomenon to create a logically precise, internally consistent standard against which real cases can be compared -- a tool of comparative analysis, not a claim that the construct exists in reality. Not the colloquial sense of 'ideal type' as a person's preferred kind of romantic partner.
nodes.source_hint: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy 'Max Weber'; general sociology-methods textbooks' treatment of the ideal type.
nodes.rationale: C1 edge-demand: the ideal type is Max Weber's foundational methodological device, anchoring field:sociology (already reviewed) and completing a theory-concept-plus-founder triangle with person:max-weber. C3: a bounded methodological construct, not a subfield.
nodes.uncertainty: 'Ideal type' is also a common English phrase (a person's preferred kind of romantic partner), a genuine homonym-collision risk for a resolver matching on the plain label alone; the referent is written to disambiguate explicitly toward Weber's Idealtypus.

nodes.referent: Adam Smith's economic concept (Wealth of Nations, 1776, opening chapters, the pin-factory example) that splitting production into specialized, repeated tasks performed by different workers increases productivity and output -- an argument about economic efficiency and the extent of the market. Distinct from Emile Durkheim's later sociological treatise 'The Division of Labour in Society' (1893), which analyzes social solidarity rather than economic efficiency.
nodes.source_hint: General economics textbooks' treatment of Adam Smith and the division of labour; Encyclopedia Britannica 'division of labour' and 'Adam Smith'.
nodes.rationale: C1 edge-demand: division of labour is one of Adam Smith's central economic arguments, anchoring field:economics (already reviewed) and completing a theory-concept-plus-founder triangle with person:adam-smith, alongside the existing concept:invisible-hand (a different Smith concept about market coordination rather than specialization -- no overlap).
nodes.uncertainty: Two real referent risks: (1) earlier writers (Mandeville, Petty, and ancient sources such as Plato and Xenophon) discussed specialization before Smith, so 'founded' reflects Smith's canonical systematic economic treatment rather than the bare idea's origin; (2) Emile Durkheim's distinct sociological treatise shares the exact phrase but analyzes social solidarity, not economic efficiency -- a resolver could plausibly surface the Durkheim referent instead of the Smith one, addressed explicitly in the referent above.

nodes.referent: Cardinality as Georg Cantor founded it in set theory: the property of a set corresponding to its 'size', defined via the existence of a bijection between sets (two sets have the same cardinality iff a one-to-one correspondence exists between them) -- the concept that let Cantor prove some infinite sets (e.g. the reals) are strictly larger than others (e.g. the naturals). Distinct from 'cardinal number' (the specific number-object, e.g. aleph-null, used to label a cardinality) and from 'transfinite number' (Cantor's broader umbrella term covering both transfinite cardinals and transfinite ordinals together, not size-comparison specifically).
nodes.source_hint: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entries on set theory and on Georg Cantor; general set-theory textbooks' treatment of cardinality via bijection.
nodes.rationale: C1 edge-demand: cardinality is Cantor's foundational innovation underlying subfield:set-theory (already reviewed), completing a theory-concept-plus-founder triangle with person:georg-cantor; re-examined per this batch's order after being held in concept-wave2-v1 for a three-way referent ambiguity. This batch resolves that ambiguity by deliberately choosing the size-comparison/bijection sense of 'cardinality' (Cantor's 1874-1895 result that infinite sets can be compared and some are strictly larger than others) as the intended referent, distinct from 'cardinal number' and 'transfinite number' -- the size-comparison sense is the specific, sourceable result standardly credited to Cantor as his founding contribution. C3: a bounded mathematical concept, not the subfield itself.
nodes.uncertainty: This is a knowledge-only, no-network re-examination of a previously-held candidate; the chosen referent is my best judgment of which of the three related senses the corpus should carry, but I cannot verify live whether an entity matching exactly this sense (as opposed to 'cardinal number' or 'transfinite number') actually exists as a separate, well-populated referent -- if a resolver cannot find a referent-precise match distinct from those two neighbors, this should be held again rather than forced through.

nodes.referent: Boolean algebra as George Boole's specific formal algebraic system of logic (An Investigation of the Laws of Thought, 1854): a two-valued algebra with operations corresponding to AND/OR/NOT obeying specific axiomatic laws, used to represent and manipulate logical propositions symbolically. This is the formal system/structure itself -- not the broader mathematical branch or subdiscipline that studies such structures in general, which is a disciplinary area already covered by subfield:mathematical-logic in this corpus.
nodes.source_hint: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy 'Boole, George'; general mathematical-logic textbooks' treatment of Boolean algebra as a formal system for propositional logic.
nodes.rationale: C1 edge-demand: Boolean algebra is George Boole's specific formal algebraic system for logic, completing a theory-concept-plus-founder triangle with person:george-boole; re-examined per this batch's order after being held in concept-wave2-v1 because the strongest identity candidate found then typed as a disciplinary referent ('branch of mathematics'). This batch deliberately targets the formal-system sense -- the specific algebraic structure/laws Boole devised -- rather than the branch of mathematics that studies such structures, which the corpus already covers via subfield:mathematical-logic; a concept naming a bounded formal system (mirroring concept:lambda-calculus and concept:turing-machine, both formal-system concepts already reviewed in this corpus) is the correct grain, not a second discipline label.
nodes.uncertainty: The underlying identity-resolution risk that caused the original hold may recur: if 'Boolean algebra' resolves, live, to only a single candidate entity whose primary type is a disciplinary/branch-of-mathematics one (with no distinct formal-system-sense entity available), this candidate should be held again rather than admitted under a referent that does not actually match anything resolvable -- I cannot verify this without network access, so the risk is stated honestly rather than resolved.

nodes.referent: The theory of relativity in physics: the framework comprising special relativity (1905) and general relativity (1915), overwhelmingly credited to Albert Einstein, describing the relativity of simultaneity/motion, spacetime as a unified structure, and gravitation as spacetime curvature. Not any single precursor's contribution to relativistic electrodynamics (e.g. Lorentz's or Poincare's separate work), and not the unrelated philosophical/sociological doctrine of relativism.
nodes.source_hint: General physics textbooks' treatment of special and general relativity; Encyclopedia Britannica 'relativity'.
nodes.rationale: C1 edge-demand: the theory of relativity is one of physics' foundational 20th-century theories, anchoring field:physics (already reviewed) via a clean part_of edge. C3: a bounded scientific theory, not a subfield of physics.
nodes.uncertainty: The candidate's named person, Henri Poincare, is NOT the mainstream-credited founder of relativity -- that credit belongs to Albert Einstein, who is currently absent from this corpus entirely (no person:albert-einstein node exists, confirmed against data/nodes.json). Poincare made real, well-documented, independently verifiable contributions to the surrounding mathematics/physics (the relativity principle, naming the Lorentz transformation, the group later called the Poincare group), reflected in this batch as an `influenced` edge rather than `founded_or_formalized`, to avoid crediting him as (co-)founder -- a position associated with a minority/disputed historiographical claim (the Einstein-Poincare priority question), not the mainstream view. Because Einstein is absent, this concept currently has no founder edge at all in the corpus, which a reader could misread as Poincare being the primary figure; that gap should be closed by a future batch adding person:albert-einstein and a founded_or_formalized edge from him, not by this batch's influenced edge alone.

nodes.referent: Biological evolution: the scientific theory/process that populations of organisms change in their heritable characteristics across successive generations, and that all species descend with modification from common ancestors -- the general theory established as science chiefly by Charles Darwin (On the Origin of Species, 1859). Distinct from natural selection (the specific mechanism Darwin proposed for evolutionary change, already a separate concept node in this corpus) and from evolutionary biology (the academic field that studies evolution).
nodes.source_hint: Encyclopedia Britannica 'Charles Darwin' and 'evolution'; general biology textbooks' treatment of the theory of evolution.
nodes.rationale: C1 edge-demand: evolution is the general scientific theory anchoring subfield:evolutionary-biology (already reviewed), completing a theory-concept-plus-founder triangle with person:charles-darwin, on the same 'theory of X + field + founder' pattern as the other historical-science candidates in this batch (conservation of mass, cell theory, germ theory, uniformitarianism).
nodes.uncertainty: Real overlap risk with the already-reviewed concept:natural-selection, which carries the identical endpoint pair (person:charles-darwin via founded_or_formalized, subfield:evolutionary-biology via part_of): 'evolution' (the general theory that species change over time via descent with modification, of which natural selection is one -- not the only -- mechanism in the modern synthesis) and 'natural selection' (the specific mechanism) are distinct referents in standard biology reference works, but QC should confirm they are genuinely two distinct external entities and not a duplicate pairing before promoting both. Evolutionary ideas also predate Darwin (Lamarck, Erasmus Darwin, Chambers's Vestiges), so 'founded' reflects Darwin giving evolution its first rigorous, evidence-backed scientific formulation rather than originating the bare idea.
